title: Finding similar items: shingling, MinHash, and LSH
summary: Follow the official Lecture 2 pipeline from shingled sets to MinHash signatures, LSH candidate generation, and exact verification.
objectives: Relate MinHash collision probability to Jaccard similarity
Explain false positives and false negatives

sections.title: Probability checkpoint
sections.body: For one MinHash permutation, $\Pr[h(A)=h(B)]=J(A,B)$. With $b$ bands of $r$ rows and similarity $s$, the LSH candidate probability is $1-(1-s^r)^b$.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture and assignment material define the current study target; the MMDS index is attached as labeled depth, not merged into lecture scope.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which similarity is estimated by MinHash collision probability?
contrastDrills.explanation: A random-permutation MinHash collision estimates Jaccard similarity for sets.

contrastDrills.prompt: What is LSH banding primarily used for?
contrastDrills.explanation: LSH makes near-neighbor search cheaper by generating candidates; exact similarity can follow.

contrastDrills.prompt: A dissimilar pair passes the LSH candidate filter. What is this?
contrastDrills.explanation: The filter admitted a pair that is not truly similar; verification controls the cost of this error.

contrastDrills.prompt: If a document contains the same shingle twice, what does the basic set-shingling representation keep?
contrastDrills.explanation: A set records membership, so duplicate occurrences collapse to one element. A multiset would retain multiplicity and requires a different similarity treatment.
contrastDrills.misconception: Counting repeated shingle occurrences while silently using set Jaccard or basic MinHash.
contrastDrills.repair: Write down the representation first: set means membership only; multiset means membership plus count.

contrastDrills.pair: Row vs band vs whole LSH collision
contrastDrills.prompt: Two signatures have similarity s, with r rows per band and b bands. Which expression is the probability that they become an LSH candidate?
choices: $1-(1-s^r)^b$ for at least one matching band
contrastDrills.explanation: One row agrees with probability s, every row in one band agrees with probability $s^r$, and at least one of b bands agrees with probability $1-(1-s^r)^b$.
contrastDrills.misconception: Using the one-row collision probability as if it were the whole LSH candidate probability, or forgetting the complement across bands.
contrastDrills.repair: Name the event before calculating: row = s, one band = $s^r$, whole filter = at least one band = $1-(1-s^r)^b$.

contrastDrills.prompt: Keeping the total number of signature rows fixed, what usually happens when we use more LSH bands with fewer rows per band?
choices: Candidate precision increases because fewer pairs can match a band
Candidate precision decreases because more pairs can pass at least one band
Precision and recall are both unchanged
The filter becomes exact and needs no verification
contrastDrills.explanation: Fewer rows per band make a full-band match easier, and more bands create more chances for a match. This usually increases recall but also admits more false positives, lowering candidate precision.
contrastDrills.misconception: Assuming more bands means a stricter filter without accounting for the easier per-band match.
contrastDrills.repair: With total rows fixed, more bands means smaller r: easier band collisions, higher candidate recall, and usually lower precision.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Estimate Jaccard similarity between large shingle sets using compact signatures instead of comparing every shingle directly.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: Each document is represented as a set of shingles, the permutations or hash functions are sufficiently random, and the same row construction is used for both documents.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: For one random permutation, the probability that two minimum-hash values collide equals their Jaccard similarity.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: For each permutation $\pi$, store the minimum hashed shingle; estimate $J(A,B)$ by the fraction of signature rows whose minimum values agree.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: treating a shingle set as a multiset, using cosine instead of Jaccard, or reading one observed collision as an exact similarity.

algorithmNotes.problemDefinition: Reduce near-neighbour search cost by generating likely similar pairs before exact similarity verification.
algorithmNotes.assumptions: The signature is divided into b bands of r rows, band events are treated as independent for the probability calculation, and a candidate is not automatically a true neighbour.
algorithmNotes.coreInvariant: A pair passes the candidate filter when at least one complete band matches; a single row match is not the whole LSH event.
algorithmNotes.formulaAlgorithm: With signature similarity s, one row collides with probability $s$, one band with $s^r$, and at least one of b bands with $1-(1-s^r)^b$.
algorithmNotes.failureModes: Common mistakes: confusing row, band, and whole-filter probabilities; assuming more bands always improve precision; or skipping exact verification.

math.explanation: Under a random permutation, the probability that the minimum hashed element agrees is exactly the Jaccard similarity. Repeating permutations gives an estimator whose collision frequency approaches $J(A,B)$.
math.name: MinHash collision identity
math.purpose: Use it to estimate Jaccard similarity from repeated minimum-hash collisions.

math.explanation: A band matches when all $r$ rows in that band match. The pair becomes a candidate if at least one of the $b$ bands matches, so compute one-minus-the-probability that every band fails.
math.name: LSH candidate probability
math.purpose: Use it to quantify the false-positive/false-negative trade-off created by bands and rows.
math.caveat: LSH trades false positives and false negatives by changing $b$ and $r$; it is not an exact similarity test.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why can LSH return a false positive even when the exact Jaccard similarity is low?
criticalQuestions.angle: Inspect the event 'at least one band matches' rather than treating a candidate as a confirmed neighbor.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A random collision in one band is enough to pass the candidate filter. Exact similarity must be computed afterward if the application needs precision.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What happens when you increase the number of rows per band while keeping the number of bands fixed?
criticalQuestions.angle: Examine the exponent $s^r$ and discuss the competing effect on similar and dissimilar pairs.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The threshold becomes sharper: high-similarity pairs are more likely to match a full band, while moderate-similarity pairs are less likely to pass.
